title: Slot vs Tiling: latency & cost scratchpad
body:
Purpose:
Quick, experiment-forward note comparing two scheduling heuristics we keep debating: fixed slot allocation (slotization) vs tiling (pack variable-length requests into tiling windows). Focus: microburst behavior, p95/p99 tail, and dollars-per-1k-queries for mixed session workloads.

Context & setup:
- Hardware: A100s (single-GPU serving node) with standard KV cache enabled.
- Model: open-llm-7b-ish, FP16, typical prompt length distribution from product telemetry (see Session Mix below).
- Two runtime modes implemented in the prototype branch:
  * slotization: allocator creates N fixed time slots per GPU; requests are admitted into next slot; leftover capacity dropped to opportunistic short-running requests.
  * tiling: sliding windows of 50ms that tile requests by token slices; attempts to pack varied sequence lengths to reduce wasted FLOPs.
- Measurement window: 2 hours, synthetic replay of sampled customer traces (week-of-2028-09-20), and 30 runs per scenario.

Session mixes used (derived from telemetry):
- Mix A (chatty): 60% short-turn (<=16 tokens), 30% medium (17-128), 10% long (>128). Burstiness: 4x baseline peak for 5s every minute.
- Mix B (sustained): 10% short, 40% medium, 50% long. Low burst amplitude, steady 0.8x baseline concurrency.
- Mix C (spiky): 80% short, 15% medium, 5% long; microbursts: 20x baseline peak, duration 200-800ms.

What I measured (aggregate):
- p50/p95/p99 latency in ms (inference only, excludes network stack)
- dollars per 1K queries (amortized using runtime GPU seconds and our internal cost model)
- slot waste: fraction of slot time filled with idle cycles that tiling would have reused

ASCII summary table (median of runs):

Scenario | Mode     | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | $/1k q | slot-waste(% or n/a)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Mix A    | slot     | 18      | 92      | 240     | 1.85   | 28%
Mix A    | tiling   | 20      | 78      | 160     | 1.62   | 6%
Mix B    | slot     | 45      | 110     | 310     | 2.05   | 22%
Mix B    | tiling   | 43      | 102     | 260     | 1.98   | 9%
Mix C    | slot     | 12      | 340     | 1100    | 3.40   | 64%
Mix C    | tiling   | 14      | 120     | 320     | 1.90   | 12%

Notes on table: slotization tends to give better p50 on low-latency short-turn steady loads (Mix C p50 12ms vs 14ms) because slots can be tuned to favor micro short requests, but the tail suffers badly when bursts exceed admission capacity — slot queues spike and cause p99 to blow up. Tiling smooths the tail by pulling work into windows and using leftover compute across requests. The cost model shows tiling often reduces $/1k by 10-45% depending on burstiness because it reduces wasted cycles.

Text heatmap-ish snapshot (approx p99 delta slot->tiling, color-coded verbally):
- Mix A: p99 improves by ~33% ("moderate green").
- Mix B: p99 improves by ~16% ("light green").
- Mix C: p99 improves by ~71% ("strong green").

Microburst behavior drilldown (Mix C example):
- Burst amplitude 20x for 400ms.
- slot: during burst, per-slot admission limit hits 3x normal; excess requests are queued; queue depth increases up to 200ms backlog, cold KV-cache misses rise 3x -> p95/p99 balloon. Observed transient kernel-switch costs (preemption) increase tail.
- tiling: packs short-turn requests into existing windows; amortization reduces kernel-launchs by ~40% in burst -> tail reduced and fewer KV misses per request.

Costs and utilization tradeoffs:
- Slotization pros: predictable per-request median, simpler scheduling, easier QoS isolation for tenants (can pin slots).
- Slotization cons: suffers from slot-waste under uneven sequence length distributions and extreme microbursts; tail cost is volatile.
- Tiling pros: higher GPU utilization, better tail under bursty short-turn heavy mixes, lower $/1k on average.
- Tiling cons: more complex packing logic; potential head-of-line blocking if long sequences dominate a tile; slightly higher p50 in some short-turn corner cases.

Small table: utilization & kernel launch counts (relative)
Scenario | Mode   | GPU util (%) | kernel-launches/sec
---------------------------------------------------
Mix A    | slot   | 72           | 18
Mix A    | tiling | 84           | 11
Mix C    | slot   | 46           | 42
Mix C    | tiling | 78           | 16

Interpreting the numbers: tiling increases utilization consistently and reduces kernel launches which correlates with reduced tail due to less preemption and fewer cold-starts for per-request contexts.

Developer/ops considerations (notes to self):
- Complexity: tiling requires careful fairness heuristics (avoid starving long sessions). Need admission thresholds that detect long-request dominance and fall back to per-request slots for those.
- Observability: telemetry must expose tile composition (number short vs long), tile fill ratio, and per-tile p99 to debug regressions.
- Backpressure & SLOs: for enterprise tenants with strict p99 SLOs, slotization + dedicated slot reservations may still be necessary. Consider hybrid: tiled default with reserved slots for SLO-bound tenants.

Open questions / experiments to run next:
1) Hybrid policies: evaluate "tiling with reserved slot slices" where N% capacity is reserved for pinned slots and remaining capacity tiles — measure p99 and cost across mixes.
2) Head-of-line mitigation: simulate timeout-based tile eviction for long sequences to avoid blocking; quantify p50 impact on short requests.
3) Vary tile window sizes (25ms/50ms/100ms) for Mix C bursts under different KV-hit scenarios; quantify delta in $/1k.
4) Multi-tenant skew: run experiments with a single noisy tenant injecting medium-long sequences while others are short-turn heavy — measure cross-tenant tail amplification.
5) Measure impact under lower-precision quant (4-bit) since tiling might increase memory/reg load patterns that change quantization benefits.

Quick recommendations for the product brief:
- For hosted API default: use tiling for general-purpose tenants (better expected p99 and cost), expose "low-latency reserved slots" as a premium control to lock a fraction of capacity to pinned tenants.
- For Dedicated: surface config UI to toggle mode and pick tile window; offer guided recommendations based on observed session-mix during onboarding.
- For Private: provide a telemetry bundle and a rule-of-thumb: if short-turn fraction >70% and microburst amplitude >8x, enable tiling; otherwise allow slots if tenant explicitly opts-in.

Unresolved items (notes):
- Need to reconcile our cost model with cloud billing granularity for Dedicated (per-GPU-hour) to ensure $/1k numbers scale to multi-GPU pools.
- Validate with multimodal token mixes (embedding+chat) — tiling semantics differ when some requests are CPU-bound.

Appendix: quick ascii chart (tile fill ratio vs p99 for Mix C):
Tile fill ratio | p99(ms)
-------------------------
0.2            | 1100
0.4            | 640
0.6            | 360
0.8            | 300
0.95           | 280

- This is approximate from runs: the p99 drops rapidly as tile fill increases; marginal returns >0.8.

References & links:
- see linked_artifacts above for source runs + replay script
- quick PR (github:repo/PR#1987) contains prototype tiling implementation and perf harness.

Last quick thoughts:
- Messaging: call the feature "adaptive tiling" in product collateral, emphasize "tail-first cost savings".
- We should get a short demo (30s replay) for the next eng-all-hands showing Mix C burst with slot vs tiling; visual p99 spike is compelling.

-- end of scratchpad --
